1.say: This sentence is eighty words long. Count the clauses. Four. But I followed all of them. Then it is not too long. Length is not the fault. Losing the reader is the fault. What keeps it standing? The subject arrives early and never changes. Every clause hangs on the same hook. The one on page five is forty words and I lost it twice. Because the subject moves. Three different people are doing things and the reader has to hold all three at once. So should I cut it into short ones? A short sentence after a long one is the strongest thing on the page. A page of short ones reads like a list of orders. Sarah writes very short. Sarah writes short in reviews and long in letters. What a short sentence costs you is the relation: it cannot show how two things are joined.

grammar.label: the long sentence that stays clear
grammar.form: coordination and subordination controlled by punctuation and parallelism
grammar.meaning: holds many clauses without losing the reader

explanation.en: A sentence can run to eighty words and stay perfectly clear, and another can lose the reader at twenty. Length is not the variable; structure is. The clear long sentence has one main clause, keeps its subject and verb close together, and hangs everything else off a visible frame. The unclear one buries the verb.
explanation.uz: Gap sakson so'z bo'lib ham aniq qolishi mumkin, boshqasi yigirmada o'quvchini yo'qotadi. Masala uzunlikda emas, tuzilishda: bitta bosh gap va ega bilan kesim yonma-yon.

grammar.positive_example: The report, which took two years and cost more than the bridge it was written about, recommended a survey.
grammar.negative_example: The report, which took two years, and which, because of the delay that the second inspection, itself delayed, caused, cost more than the bridge, recommended a survey.

l1_notes.uz: O'zbek tilida uzun gaplar ergash gaplar bilan quriladi va fe'l oxirida keladi; ingliz tilida bu o'quvchini yo'qotadi.

grammar.label: the short sentence and what it costs
grammar.form: a sequence of short main clauses with no subordination
grammar.meaning: gains force and loses the relations between ideas

explanation.en: Short sentences hit harder and say less. 'He resigned. The fund closed. Nobody was told.' — the reader must supply the causal links, and different readers will supply different ones. That vagueness is an effect in fiction and a defect in a report. Prose made only of short sentences is not plain; it is unfinished.
explanation.uz: Qisqa gaplar kuchliroq uradi va kamroq aytadi. Sabab-oqibatni o'quvchi o'zi to'ldiradi, va turli o'quvchi turlicha to'ldiradi.

grammar.positive_example: He resigned in March. The fund closed in April. The minutes record no connection.
grammar.negative_example: He resigned. The fund closed. Nobody was told. It was all connected. Obviously.

l1_notes.uz: Qisqa gaplar ketma-ketligi ingliz jurnalistikasida uslub; hisobotda esa mantiqiy bog'lanishni yo'qotadi.

body.text: Then it is not too long. Length is not the fault. Losing the reader is the fault.

body.speaker: Aziz
body.text: The subject arrives early and never changes. Every clause hangs on the same hook.

body.speaker: Dilnoza
body.text: The one on page five is forty words and I lost it twice.

body.speaker: Aziz
body.text: Because the subject moves. Three different people are doing things and the reader has to hold all three at once.

body.speaker: Dilnoza
body.text: So should I cut it into short ones?

body.speaker: Aziz
body.text: A short sentence after a long one is the strongest thing on the page. A page of short ones reads like a list of orders.

body.speaker: Aziz
body.text: Sarah writes short in reviews and long in letters. What a short sentence costs you is the relation: it cannot show how two things are joined.
